t: Check if Two Chessboard Squares Have the Same Color
o: Square color alternates like a checkerboard: square (file c, rank r) has color determined by the parity of (c + r). Two squares share a color iff (file1 + rank1) ≡ (file2 + rank2) (mod 2). Convert letters/digits to their ordinal codes and compare parities.
k: Use character codes directly: (c1[0] + c1[1]) % 2 == (c2[0] + c2[1]) % 2.
No board representation needed — pure arithmetic.

a.i: Sum the character codes of file and rank for each square; the two squares match color exactly when the sums have equal parity.
a.t: O(1) — constant number of character operations

a.i: Convert file to 0–7 and rank to 0–7 explicitly, then compare (file + rank) parities. More readable and extensible (e.g., if you later need the actual color name).
s: f = c[0] - 'a', r = c[1] - '1' for each coordinate.

w: Trivial problem; the only risk is an off-by-one in the parity convention — but since we only compare two squares, any consistent convention works. Sanity-check with the examples: a1 and c3 both give even parity (true); a1 vs h3 differ (false). Follow-up: return the actual color names, or handle coordinates on an N×N board.
